You speak in my sleep and I wake slow. I do not throw grain at every shadow.

Tell me plainly—how do you know Wewush is hungry? Where is that village hidden from my scouts? Bring me one true sign in the waking world, and I will send men.

If your tale is true, we will not turn our backs. I will send two steady adults with an envoy-load of grain and seed, and a cloth to mark us friend; they will stay the week and learn how we keep food safe for lean times. If they truly are starving, I will order more grain sent until the spirits or the land set them right.

Wind that moves over our roofs, I know the feel of you — the lift of smoke, the sway of rafters, the sound you make in thatch at night. You are a thing I can touch on my face and hear on my roof; not a stranger spirit in a bright place.

Tell me plainly: do you bring warning or blessing? Will you carry water in the sky to make the year kind, or do you come with a storm that will tear our tents and waste our seed? If you have news of another place—fresh water, standing trees, wild herds—speak so I may heed it.

You speak long watch, spirit. I will answer plain.

We hunger not. Grain and hides sit like a mountain. What thins my heart is wood and stone — wood for houses and fences, stone for heavy work — these stores are small. Also metal-less flint is enough, but strong hands are few: ten grown to set tasks.

If your rain comes in summer, tell me this: will it fall soon enough for a seed sown now to ripen? And where shall I send my people to find more wood or stone without leaving the food unmade? Show some sign, and I will listen.

You say you watched before my grandmother. I do not forget promises easily, but I do not plant on a dream alone.

The thing that worries me most now is our wood. We have food enough, hides plenty, cloth enough; but only fifty-two wood will not mend poor roofs or build much new shelter when wind breaks things, nor last if we must turn to more drying, boats, or a stockade. If the summer will bring rain, tell me this: will it come steady enough for young grain to root and not drown? Show me a sign I can watch by day.

I will not give all my store on a whisper. If they are near and truly starving, I will send grain enough to keep a few for the season and two able envoys to meet them, trade or teach better ways, and make a bond of friendship so the aid does not become endless need. If they are far or come with men who would take by force, we will not waste food. Answer me so I may choose.

Wind that walks over our roofs — I know your sound, your cool hand on my face when the sun is high and the long grasses bend. You are old as rocks and younger than a child’s breath; you come with storm and with salt and with the smell of distant water.

Tell me plainly: do you bring news of weather to come, or of places beyond our hills? Will you be friend and carry seed and warm smoke, or will you test our roofs and scatter our stores? If you mean me harm, speak so I may ready my people; if you mean good, tell where we should send a pair of ears to listen.
